newsitem.title: UK: WEEK AHEAD - Politics in Europe, quieter times in US.
newsitem.headline: WEEK AHEAD - Politics in Europe, quieter times in US.

text.p: The aftermath of one European election and the build-up to another will be dominant themes for financial markets in the coming week, economists said on Friday. Britain's Labour party swept to power after a May 1 ballot, while in France the political dogfight is only just beginning. Data out of the U.S. will be lighter after a string of crucial numbers last week. Germany releases a clutch of figures, while the prospect of an interest rate rise in Britain will hold markets spellbound as monetary authorities get set to meet.

"The U.S. will be much quieter," said Teis Knuthsen, international economist at First Chicago in London. "The most important things will probably be the Beige Book ahead of the May 20 Federal Reserve meeting and then the quarterly refunding."
The Fed's Beige Book will be published on Wednesday and the Fed is due to meet for its Open Market Committee (FOMC) meeting on May 20.

Key data last week has left markets no closer to knowing whether the Fed will raise rates again at the meeting. U.S. employment costs were restrained, jobs growth was softer-than-expected but the April unemployment rate slid to 4.9 percent, a level not seen since December 1973.
The U.S. Treasury will auction $17.0 billion of three-year notes on Monday and $12.0 billion of 10-year notes on Tuesday.
Knuthsen said Japan was also likely to be quiet with a public holiday for Golden week early in the week.
German March industrial production and manufacturing new orders are expected from Monday on and April unemployment is due on Tuesday.
"The last German indicators we had suggested growth was slowing somewhat so the production indicators will be very important," Knuthsen said.

Britain's Labour Party's first week in power for over 18 years will be scrutinised by the financial markets this week after a gentle start with a public holiday on Monday. Among the British data due are March industrial production and manufacturing output figures on Wednesday.
The main event, however, will be the first monetary meeting between the new Chancellor, set to be Labour's Gordon Brown, and Bank of England governor Eddie George, currently scheduled for May 7.

"The most important thing will probably be whether a new Labour government will raise rates at the Brown-George meeting on May 7. It could be delayed but if not people will expect rates to go up next Wednesday," Knuthsen said.
While short sterling futures markets are pricing in a 50 basis point rise to three month money rates by expiry in the middle of June, some analysts have said they may have overdone it.

"We still think that the ultimate extent of the monetary tightening will turn out to be less than feared by the markets at present," said John Shepperd, chief economist at Yamaichi International Europe in London.

Shepperd said in a research note that a quarter point rate rise would not be surprising on Wednesday but the ultimate extent of the rise may be no more than half a point. British base rates currently stand at six percent.

Sally Wilkinson, senior economist at Daiwa Europe in London, said the French political battle will attract attention. "The French election is playing a role but I'm relatively convinced the centre-right will come back into power," she said. She said that from a political point of view the market she most wanted to keep tabs on was Italy. "There's a lot of internal political jostling going on in Italy. There's a chance (Italian Prime Minister Romano) Prodi will be forced from power." Italian final CPI data were expected on Tuesday. "They are always close to preliminary numbers but the real issue is whether seeing the final CPI will be taken as an excuse by the Bank of Italy to cut rates now that we have the lira below the central parity of 990 to the mark," Knuthsen said.
